summary:
A visitor entering Nevada is screened under the United States federal document regime, not Nevada state law. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, recognises only two sexes and directs federal agencies to a male-female binary. The State Department suspended applications for passport gender-marker changes and ended the self-identified 'X' passport option on 22 January 2025. Passports issued before January 2025 carrying a marker other than sex assigned at birth remain valid until expiry; new applications are processed only as M or F.

Visa screening carries a second exposure. Under Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 and the State Department announcement of 25 February 2025, trans athletes seeking to enter the country to compete in women's sporting events are refused visas, with applicants flagged under the internal code 'SWS25', and an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as having made a fraudulent misrepresentation, a ground for permanent bar.

Nevada's own legal environment sits at the protective end of the United States. A July 2026 national legal risk assessment places Nevada in its Low-Risk group, one tier below the most protective category, together with Arizona, Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Virginia, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia. The assessment credits the state with fairly robust non-discrimination policies covering gender identity and gender expression, while judging that Nevada falls short on healthcare equity and on protections for incarcerated transgender people.

Facilities access is not restricted by state law in Nevada. The Movement Advancement Project's Equality Map records that state bathroom and facility bans applying to transgender people in schools and government buildings exist in nine states and one territory; Nevada is not among them, and is one of the 29 states with no such ban.

State identity documents are comparatively easy to obtain and can be set apart from the federal passport. Since 2016 Nevada Vital Records issues a corrected-gender birth certificate on two affidavies alone, with sex reassignment surgery not required, and equivalent changes are available for driver's licences and state identification cards. Nevada has offered an 'X' third-gender designation on driver's licences, birth certificates and state identification cards since 2019 with no medical documentation required. That state-level 'X' option no longer has any federal counterpart, and a Nevada identity document showing a gender marker that differs from a passport will be read against the federal binary at the border.

Nevada removed the older procedural burdens on legal sex change. A law signed 22 June 2017 abolished the 1988 requirement that transgender people publish notice of their names in newspapers before changing sex on government documents.

Care access for adults in Nevada is protected by statute, but the federal floor has moved against care for minors nationwide. Nevada's Medicaid agency announced in March 2018 that it would cover sex-reassignment surgery, state law bans health insurers from discriminating against transgender patients, and a bill effective 1 January 2024 requires insurers including Medicaid to cover all medically necessary gender-affirming treatments. In June 2025 the United States Supreme Court held in United States v. Skrmetti that state bans on gender-affirming care for minors are constitutional, removing a federal constitutional obstacle to bans elsewhere while leaving Nevada's own statutory protections in force.

Two state corrections measures point in opposite directions. In May 2023 the governor signed a law protecting transgender and intersex individuals in state correctional facilities. The same year the legislature passed an omnibus bill, SB 302, shielding gender-affirming care and abortion, which the governor vetoed.

School and collegiate sport in Nevada follows sex assigned at birth. In April 2025 the Nevada Interscholastic Activities Association reversed its 2016 policy and now requires transgender athletes to compete under their sex assigned at birth. This affects scholastic competition in the state rather than visitors entering to compete, but sits alongside the federal visa refusal that does apply at entry.
tangentialFactors:
Nevada's position is an outlier in the national direction of travel. While the federal government has narrowed document and care rules since January 2025, Nevada has expanded state-level recognition: an 'X' marker on licences and birth certificates since 2019, birth certificate corrections on two affidavits since 2016, and statutory insurer coverage of gender-affirming treatment from 1 January 2024. Several states have moved the opposite way; a February 2026 Kansas law prevents transgender people from changing markers on birth certificates and driver's licences and invalidates existing documents that do not match sex assigned at birth.

A July 2026 national risk assessment flagged Idaho as the latest state rated 'Do Not Travel' for trans people, bringing that total to four states, and reported that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights nationwide. Nevada appears in the Low-Risk tier of the same assessment, below the most protective group but well clear of the states carrying such warnings.

Facility access is the sharpest sub-national divergence. Nine states and one territory restrict transgender people's use of public bathrooms and facilities by gender identity in schools and some government buildings, and in some circumstances treat trans bathroom use as a criminal offence; in April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol. Nevada imposes no comparable restriction.

Custody remains the weak point even in a protective state. The July 2026 assessment names Nevada's treatment of incarcerated transgender people as a shortfall alongside healthcare equity. Federal custody inside the state stands under federal policy rather than Nevada statutes, and national reporting on federal prisons and immigration detention describes hormone withdrawal, forced hair cutting and denial of care for transgender detainees.

The Supreme Court's June 2025 Skrmetti ruling means the state-level protections a visitor can rely on in Nevada are not guaranteed elsewhere in the country, and that a Nevadan's own protections rest on statute rather than a federal constitutional floor.

outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the inventory does not document whether Nevada has taken any state-level administrative or legal response to Executive Order 14168 or to the federal passport marker suspension, such as state-issued guidance on mismatched documents or litigation by the state attorney general. Not sourced here.

Unresolved: the July 2026 assessment's finding that Nevada falls short on healthcare equity and on protections for incarcerated transgender people is stated without the underlying incidents or outcomes. What specifically is rated short of adequate in those two areas is not sourced in this inventory.

Unresolved: federal custody inside Nevada is not covered. Federal prison and immigration detention policy applies to anyone held federally in the state regardless of Nevada statutes, but the inventory contains no Nevada-specific reporting on conditions, care provision or transfer practice.

Not sourced: the effect of the June 2025 Skrmetti decision on gender-affirming care for minors in Nevada specifically. The ruling permits state bans generally; whether Nevada's statutory treatment of minors' care has been challenged or restricted is not addressed.

The Movement Advancement Project's Equality Map is the comparison source used to place Nevada among states without facility bans; its underlying criteria for counting a ban were not examined in this pass.
